subject: Science
title: Force and Pressure
learningOutcomes: Define force and describe balanced and unbalanced forces and their effects.
Explain resultant force and state Newton’s first law of motion.
Explain upthrust and use density to predict floating and sinking.
Define pressure, use pressure = force ÷ area, and explain everyday examples.
Describe pressure in gases and liquids, and how hydraulic machines multiply force.

sections.heading: Forces: Balanced and Unbalanced
sections.body: A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons (N), and forces always act in pairs. When the forces on an object are balanced (equal and opposite) there is no resultant force, so the object stays still or moves at a steady speed in a straight line — this is Newton’s first law. When forces are unbalanced they leave a resultant force (greater force minus smaller force) that starts a stationary object moving or speeds up a moving object in the direction of the resultant.

sections.heading: Floating, Upthrust and Density
sections.body: A fluid pushes up on an object with a force called upthrust, which equals the weight of the fluid displaced (Archimedes’ principle). A boat floats because the upthrust from the water it displaces balances its weight. Density is the mass per unit volume (density = mass ÷ volume). Water’s density is about 1 g/cm³; objects less dense than water float and denser objects sink. Denser liquids, such as sea water, give greater upthrust.

sections.heading: Pressure in Solids
sections.body: Pressure is the force acting per unit area: pressure = force ÷ area, measured in pascals (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m². A small area gives a high pressure (stiletto heels, a sharp knife, a nail tip), while a large area gives a low pressure (a bed of nails, wide tyres, a camel’s feet).

sections.heading: Pressure in Gases
sections.body: Gas molecules are far apart and move fast in all directions, so a gas can be compressed and fills its container. Atmospheric pressure, caused by the weight of the air above, is about 100 kPa at sea level. If a gas is squashed into a smaller volume its pressure rises (pressure × volume stays constant — Boyle’s Law) and it heats up because the molecules move faster.

sections.heading: Pressure in Liquids
sections.body: The weight of a liquid presses on the base of its container, and the pressure increases with depth and with the density of the liquid. Liquid pressure acts in all directions and does not depend on the shape of the container. This is why dam walls are thicker at the bottom and submarines need strong walls.

sections.heading: Hydraulic Machines
sections.body: Hydraulic machines use a liquid to transmit force. Because liquids are very hard to compress and pass pressure on equally throughout, a small input force on a small piston creates a pressure that acts on a larger piston to give a much larger output force — so the machine is a force multiplier. Car brakes work this way, transmitting pressure through the brake fluid.

definitions.definition: A push or a pull on an object, measured in newtons (N).
Equal and opposite forces that cancel out, so the motion does not change.
The single net force from unbalanced forces (greater minus smaller).
The upward push of a fluid, equal to the weight of fluid displaced.
The mass per unit volume of a substance (density = mass ÷ volume).
The force acting on a surface per unit area (pressure = force ÷ area).
The unit of pressure; 1 Pa = 1 N/m².
A machine that uses a liquid to transmit and multiply force.

examTips: Learn the three formulas: pressure = force ÷ area, density = mass ÷ volume, and resultant force = greater − smaller force.
Remember the rule: an object floats if its density is less than water (1 g/cm³) and sinks if it is greater.
Small area → high pressure; large area → low pressure. Use this for every "why" question (heels, nails, tyres, feet).
Hydraulics need an incompressible liquid — a gas would just squash, so it cannot transmit the force.

interactiveLesson.instructions: Explore the forces and pressures acting on a floating boat and a hydraulic jack. Select every hotspot to continue.

hotspots.label: Weight (down)
hotspots.fact: The boat’s weight is a downward force caused by gravity, measured in newtons.

hotspots.label: Upthrust (up)
hotspots.fact: The water pushes up with an upthrust equal to the weight of the water the boat displaces.

hotspots.label: Balanced Forces
hotspots.fact: The upward upthrust balances the downward weight, so the boat floats steadily.

hotspots.label: Displaced Water
hotspots.fact: A floating boat pushes aside a large volume of water; more load means more water displaced.

hotspots.label: Pressure = Force ÷ Area
hotspots.fact: Pressure depends on the force and the area it acts on — the key idea for solids, liquids and gases.

items: This creates a pressure in the liquid

correctOrder: A small force pushes the narrow piston

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A car has a forward force of 800 N and a backward force of 1000 N. What happens?

options: It slows down (200 N resultant backwards)

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Backward force is greater, so the 200 N resultant slows the car down.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A steel ship floats even though steel is denser than water because:

options: It is hollow and displaces a large volume of water

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Its shape displaces enough water for the upthrust to balance its weight.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Input 12 N on 0.01 m²; output piston area 0.1 m². Output force?
A 550 N woman stands on one stiletto heel of area 1 cm² (0.0001 m²). The pressure is:
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: 550 ÷ 0.0001 = 5 500 000 Pa — a huge pressure from a tiny area.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: Why would a hydraulic brake filled with air instead of fluid fail?

options: Air compresses, so it squashes instead of transmitting the force

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: A gas compresses, so the pressure is not transmitted — the brakes feel spongy and weak.
